section_summary: This section opens with Ambassador Joseph C. Grew’s detailed report on Japan’s coal and electric-power shortages, followed by translated regulations restricting electricity use and a newspaper clipping on plans to increase coal production. It then contains an intelligence telegram alleging that Japanese authorities encouraged pessimistic foreign reporting about Japan’s economy, together with several State and War Department memoranda assessing and criticizing Lieutenant Norman E. Towson’s economic analysis. The final and largest subfile is the opening portion of Towson’s study of Japan’s foreign trade, strategic-material dependence, gold and foreign-exchange reserves, borrowing capacity, public finance, and inflation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4494: Japan's Shortages—Coal and Electric Power
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the causes, industrial effects, and governmental handling of Japan's severe coal and electric-power shortages.
subfiles.summary: Grew attributes the power crisis to inadequate expansion of generating capacity, rapid state-directed industrialization, drought, and an immediate shortage of usable coal. He describes defective coal-price and permit controls, poor-quality output, transportation bottlenecks, and severe power reductions affecting textiles, chemicals, iron, and aluminum production. He concludes that piecemeal wartime controls cannot solve Japan's shortages without an integrated economic plan and a better balance between industrial ambitions and national capacity.

subfiles.title: Translations of Ministerial Notices Nos. 3685 and 3686
subfiles.about: Prohibits selected nonessential uses and new supplies of electricity from January 1, 1940.
subfiles.summary: Notice no. 3685 bars electricity consumption for neon signs, decorations, advertising, most outdoor and garden lighting, and multi-bulb streetlights. Notice no. 3686 prevents suppliers from furnishing electricity for such uses as electric baths, added heating and cooking equipment, new refrigerators, garden pumps, and most elevators and escalators. Prefectural governors or the Tokyo Metropolitan Police superintendent could authorize exceptions.

subfiles.title: Notification No. 232 of the Ministry of Communications
subfiles.to: Electric-power consumers in the designated districts
subfiles.about: Establishes compulsory limits on electricity consumption effective February 10, 1940.
subfiles.summary: The notification applies consumption limits under the Imperial Ordinance for the Control of Electric Power while allowing specified ministerial, local, emergency, and self-generated-power exceptions. Its table organizes restrictions by geographic district and service classification, identifying several priority industries such as mining, petroleum, metals, shipbuilding, vehicles, chemicals, pulp, and fuel production. The final provisions explain the consumption baselines and prorating rules used to calculate monthly allowances.

subfiles.title: Table of Classification of Consumption Applicable under Regulations Pertaining to the Consumption of Electric Power
subfiles.about: Classifies military, industrial, commercial, public-utility, and domestic uses of electricity for regulatory purposes.
subfiles.summary: Classification I covers military and specially designated services. Classification II divides mining, metals, manufacturing, transportation, communications, export production, agriculture, and public enterprises into regulated groups. Classifications III and IV cover other manufacturing and business services, illumination, heaters, and motors.

subfiles.title: Notification No. 231: Table Showing Districts for the Consumption of Electric Power
subfiles.about: Defines the territorial districts to be used when imposing electricity restrictions or prohibitions.
subfiles.summary: The notification divides Hokkaido into northeastern and southwestern sections and enumerates the included historical provinces, districts, towns, and villages. It similarly identifies northern and southern portions of the northeastern district and lists the remaining Kanto, Chubu, Kinki, Chugoku, Shikoku, and Kyushu divisions. These boundaries supplied the geographic framework for applying power-control orders.

subfiles.title: Coal Increase Plan Costing ¥110,000,000 Completed for Diet
subfiles.about: Describes a Commerce and Industry Ministry plan to raise Japanese coal output by six million tons in fiscal 1940–41.
subfiles.summary: The plan combined production bounties, subsidies for new shafts and galleries, and preferential allocation of labor and materials to coal producers. It also proposed a semi-official joint sales company to pool purchases, stabilize official prices, suppress illegal transactions, discourage low-grade coal, and improve distribution. The government intended to seek Diet approval and supplementary funding.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 136 from Chungking
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Ambassador at Chungking
subfiles.about: Reports claims that Japanese authorities welcomed or encouraged pessimistic American reporting about Japan's economic condition.
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays information from the British ambassador, believed to derive from German sources in Japan, that pessimistic reports would discourage the United States from taking special measures against Japan. An Italian correspondent further claimed that Japanese authorities had urged foreign journalists to spread such reports so Americans would await an anticipated Japanese economic collapse. The message was repeated to Peiping for air transmission to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 136
subfiles.from: Department of State summary of Nelson T. Johnson's telegram
subfiles.about: Restates the allegation that Japan promoted pessimistic accounts of its economy to deter American countermeasures.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase combines both sections of Johnson's telegram into a form suitable for controlled circulation. It emphasizes that Japanese authorities allegedly wanted Americans to expect Japan's economic collapse and therefore allow events to run their course. It also records the German-source view that neither Japan's nor Germany's economy was as weak as generally believed.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Commenting on Lieutenant Towson's Economic Study
subfiles.about: Critiques Towson's assertions about cooperation with Japan, authoritarian trade practices, and the size of Japan's gold reserve.
subfiles.summary: The writer argues that accepting Japan's new order without military resistance would not require American financial cooperation or large credits. He disputes Towson's claim that multi-country trade arrangements were normal under authoritarian trade control, maintaining that bilateral balancing predominated. He also estimates Japan's end-1939 gold holdings at roughly $115 million rather than Towson's $66 million, chiefly because of differing estimates of privately held gold and transfers involving the Banks of Chosen and Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck's Comments on The Economic Position of Japan—Current Estimate
subfiles.about: Evaluates the strengths and evidentiary weaknesses of Towson's study.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck praises Towson's discussion of foreign trade, gold depletion, fiscal problems, and the general political outlook. He finds the embargo section insufficiently supported and argues that the final conclusion ventures beyond the study's economic evidence. In particular, he questions assertions about Japanese psychology, an unavoidable American policy choice, a move toward the South Pacific if Holland entered the European war, and probable Japanese military action against the United States.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Principal Conclusions of Towson's Economic Study
subfiles.about: Summarizes Towson's main findings about Japan's trade deficit, strategic reserves, foreign exchange, inflation, and possible expansion.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum regards Towson's study as generally excellent and highlights Japan's failure to obtain essential imports without spending foreign exchange, the depletion of material reserves, and an estimated gold reserve of no more than $67 million. It states that Japan might exhaust its foreign-exchange resources by the end of 1940 and notes growing inflation, though it cautions that the claim of an imminent runaway situation may be too strong. It closes with Towson's argument that economic pressure might drive Japan to seize the Dutch East Indies.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Assistant Chief of Staff, WPD, on the Economic Position of Japan
subfiles.from: J. M. Churchill, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, War Plans Division
subfiles.about: Transmits Towson's study and discusses the need for a clearly defined American policy toward Japan and East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Churchill describes Towson as well qualified and recommends serious consideration of his financial and economic conclusions while treating his political forecast as conjectural. He argues that Japan's economic vulnerability could support economic, diplomatic, or military pressure only after the United States defines realistic objectives in the Far East. The memorandum observes that American agencies and public opinion were divided and suggests that the relative strength of Japan, China, and Soviet Russia might be shaped to serve American interests and international stability.

subfiles.title: The Economic Position of Japan: Current Estimate
subfiles.from: Norman E. Towson, Far Eastern Section, Intelligence Branch, M.I.D.
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan's economic condition limits further aggression and identifies economic vulnerabilities available to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Towson warns against expecting Japan's controlled economy to collapse quickly, despite profound dependence on imported strategic materials and mounting financial strains. The portion present here analyzes Japan's adverse trade balance outside the yen bloc, unsuccessful efforts to expand Latin American commerce, shortages of petroleum and industrial minerals, and the progressive depletion of gold and other foreign-exchange assets. It argues that Japan could neither borrow substantial dollar funds nor continue covering annual external deficits for long. The domestic-finance section describes rapidly rising public debt, heavy bond issuance, currency expansion, failing price controls, black markets, commodity scarcity, and what Towson characterizes as an approaching breakdown of Japan's financial organization.
